cards.title: Roger W. Ferguson, Jr.
cards.sub: 2001 · Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
cards.body: Vice chairman of the Federal Reserve Board, in his Washington office when the second plane hit. His job that day was not repair but substitution: keep balances moving while other institutions' copies of the day's payments sat unreachable. On 12 September, discount window lending ran about $46 billion, more than two hundred times the previous month's daily average.
cards.prompt: Name the Federal Reserve vice chairman who was in Washington on 11 September 2001, and say what the Board offered banks that morning instead of trying to repair anything.
cards.answer: Roger W. Ferguson, Jr. The Board offered liquidity — 'the discount window is available to meet liquidity needs' — because what had broken was the movement of payments, not the money.

cards.title: The clearing banks evacuate
cards.sub: 11 September 2001 · Bank of New York, Lower Manhattan
cards.body: Bank of New York's funds transfer and bond clearing systems ran from 101 Barclay Street, one block north of the World Trade Center; its One Wall Street headquarters stood half a mile away. Both were evacuated. Government securities settlement fails rose from $1.7 billion a day the week of 5 September to $190 billion the week ending 19 September.
cards.prompt: Bank of New York's staff were alive and its records were intact. Give the payments figure that shows why that was not enough, and name what had actually failed.
cards.answer: It was reported overdue on $100 billion in payments during the week after 11 September 2001. What failed was the site and its connectivity — the primary and its people were in the same few blocks — not the data.

cards.title: Interagency Paper on Sound Practices
cards.sub: 7 April 2003 · Federal Reserve Board, OCC and SEC
cards.body: Issued as an attachment to Federal Reserve supervisory letter SR 03-9, and open to read today. It defines recovery-time objectives, declines to prescribe any specific technology solution, and tells core clearing and settlement organisations to put their back-up facilities past the reach of synchronous mirroring.
cards.prompt: The 2003 supervisory paper fixes one time limit and refuses to fix one distance. State the time limit, and quote the phrase the agencies used in place of a mileage.
cards.answer: Recover and resume clearing and settlement within the business day, with the goal of two hours after an event. The agencies would not 'prescribe specific mileage requirements'; instead back-up facilities must be 'well outside of the current synchronous range'.

cards.title: Why your far replica is async
cards.body: Ordering back-ups outside synchronous range turned nonzero lag into a supervised fact, and recovery-time objectives into contract terms. Hence the standard layout: semi-synchronous to a nearby replica for machine death, asynchronous to a distant one for regional disaster. RPO=0 and real distance never appear on the same line.
cards.prompt: A regulator orders your back-up site beyond the range synchronous mirroring can reach. Which durability number does that force you to publish, and what is that number physically equal to?
cards.answer: The recovery point objective. It is just the replication lag at the moment of failover — the acknowledged writes the far copy had not yet received — so RPO is measured in seconds, not chosen.
